title: Practice with children
hook: a bedtime gratitude, a walk, a story: "suffer the little children" means let them come, and Jesus took them in his arms
tomorrow: why did one desert monk run from everyone who loved him?

segments.voice: Yesterday: together. Tobias asked Sarah to rise and pray with him, and she said the amen too. Today the people in the practice get shorter.

Read "suffer the little children" to a six-year-old and watch the face. It sounds like a threat. It's a King James line, and the strange word is the whole puzzle. In Mark's Gospel, people are bringing young children to Jesus, hoping he'll touch them. And his own disciples are turning them away. Busy teacher. Important adults. Not now, kids.
screen: `SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN?` → `IT SOUNDS LIKE A THREAT.` → `NOT NOW, KIDS.`

segments.voice: In the English of the King James Bible, suffer means let, or allow. So the line reads: let the little children come. And look at what comes before it: "when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased." Not with the children. With the disciples who were guarding his time. Then he says it: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." He goes further. Whoever won't receive the kingdom as a little child won't enter it at all. And Mark closes the scene with three plain actions: "he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them." Christians read a teaching in it. Children aren't waiting at the door until they're old enough to understand. They belong already, and they're the picture of how anyone receives God: with open hands, not a finished theology. So a practice with children doesn't start with an explanation. It starts with arms and hands and a blessing, things a small body can receive. A bedtime thank-you. A short walk where you notice things together. One story, told well. Small ones, let in.
screen: `SUFFER MEANS LET.` · `HE WAS MUCH DISPLEASED.` · `OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM.` · `ARMS, HANDS, A BLESSING.` · then, large: `SMALL ONES.`

segments.voice: Count three good things from today on your fingers, the way you might with a child at bedtime: one, two, three. Keep each one small and concrete, a warm cup, a kind text, a patch of sun. Then rest your hands open in your lap.
Practice with children: a small practice a child can join, a bedtime thank-you, a walk, a story, with the children let in, not shushed out.
Something to hold: small ones. In Mark, they get arms and a blessing before any lesson. That's day 1654.

screen: `DAY 1654 COUNTS.` → `OTHERS · 2 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DID ONE DESERT MONK RUN FROM EVERYONE WHO LOVED HIM?`

howItsDone: Families on many paths keep small practices with children: a thank-you at bedtime, a blessing with a hand on the head, a story told again. Christians point to Mark 10, where Jesus takes the children in his arms and blesses them.
